t: Minimum Operations to Make Array Parity Alternating
o:
Parity alternating means adjacent elements differ in parity, i.e., the whole array follows one of two parity patterns: E,O,E,O,... or O,E,O,E,.... Each element whose parity disagrees with the chosen pattern needs exactly one ±1 operation; agreeing elements need zero. So the minimum op count is the smaller mismatch count over the two patterns.

The subtle part is answer[1]: using exactly that many operations, mismatched positions must shift by exactly ±1 (their choice) and matched positions cannot move. We must pick signs to minimize max − min. Example 1: pattern starting odd fits [-2,-3,1,4] with mismatches at indices 2,3 (values 1→2, 4→3), giving range 3−(−3)=6. Example 2: [0,2,-2] needs 1 op; changing 2 to 1 yields range 1−(−2)=3.
k: There are only two target parity patterns; the cheaper one fixes answer[0].
Given the pattern, each mismatched element independently chooses nums[i]−1 or nums[i]+1; a greedy over sorted options minimizes the resulting range.

a.n: Approach 1: Pattern enumeration plus greedy range compression
a.i: Try both patterns. For a pattern, build each index's option set: {nums[i]} if parity matches, {nums[i]−1, nums[i]+1} otherwise. Sort indices by (low, high) option and sweep, always assigning the smallest allowed value ≥ current running value. Because picks are non-decreasing and the first pick equals the global minimum low, the final pick minus the first pick is the minimal achievable range; a standard exchange argument shows this greedy is optimal and never gets stuck.
s: For each start parity p in {0,1}: count mismatches (answer[0] candidate) and build option intervals [lo,hi] per index.
Sort intervals by (lo, hi); sweep keeping cur = max(previous pick, lo); record first and last picks.
Range = last − first; among patterns with minimal ops, take the smaller range.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting the option intervals dominates; everything else is linear

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the range
a.i: Instead of the greedy sweep, binary search the minimal feasible range D: a window [x, x+D] works iff every index has an option inside it. Feasibility is checked greedily by sweeping indices sorted by their minimum option, maintaining the earliest feasible window start. This is slower (adds a log factor) but generalizes to richer option sets.
s: Binary search D over [0, max spread + 2].
Check(D): sort options by lo; sweep assigning each index the smallest option ≥ current lower bound; fail if outside the window.
Return the smallest feasible D together with the op count.
a.t: O(n log n log V) — binary search over the range multiplied by the sort-based feasibility check

w: Approach 1 is preferable: simpler and faster. Critical pitfalls: handling negative numbers' modulo (use floor-mod semantics), remembering that matched elements cannot move when the op budget is exactly minimal, and evaluating both patterns when their op counts tie. Follow-up: what if both increase and decrease by more than 1 were allowed per operation, or if the array had to remain non-negative?
